items.title: GROUP BY — summarise into groups
items.body:
## What it is
`GROUP BY` collapses rows into one row per group, paired with an **aggregate** (`SUM`, `AVG`, `COUNT`). It is the SQL pivot table — and the same split-apply-combine as pandas `groupby`.

## Why it matters
Every "per X" question — profit per sub-category, sales per region — is a GROUP BY. It's the workhorse of analytical SQL, and re-deriving your Week 1 margin finding with it proves the analysis transfers across tools (which is what makes you genuinely fluent rather than dependent on one).

## WHERE vs HAVING — the classic confusion
`WHERE` filters **rows before** grouping; `HAVING` filters **groups after** aggregating. "Orders over $500" is a WHERE; "sub-categories whose *total* profit is negative" is a HAVING (it tests an aggregate). And every column you SELECT must be either in the GROUP BY or wrapped in an aggregate — otherwise SQL doesn't know which row's value to show.

## Q1 (margin leaders) in SQL
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```sql
SELECT sub_category, SUM(profit) AS total_profit
FROM superstore
GROUP BY sub_category
ORDER BY total_profit DESC
LIMIT 5;
```
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```
sub_category  total_profit
Copiers        55617.8
Phones         44515.7
Accessories    41936.6
Paper          34053.6
Binders        30221.8
```

## The loss-makers — HAVING filters the GROUPS
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```sql
SELECT sub_category, SUM(profit) AS total_profit
FROM superstore
GROUP BY sub_category
HAVING SUM(profit) < 0
ORDER BY total_profit ASC;
```
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```
sub_category  total_profit
Tables        -17725.5
Bookcases      -3472.6
Supplies       -1189.1
```
Three sub-categories lose money overall — the same answer Excel and pandas gave, now in SQL. `HAVING` (not `WHERE`) because it tests the aggregated `SUM(profit)`.

items.title: Aggregate over time (year-over-year)
items.body:
## What it is
To see a trend you group by a **slice of the date**. In SQLite, `strftime('%Y', order_date)` extracts the year as text, and you GROUP BY that to get one total per year.

## Why it matters
"Is the business growing?" is a time question, and time questions are answered by grouping on a date part — year, quarter, month. It turns a pile of dated orders into a trend line: the Q2 year-over-year answer you computed in pandas, now in SQL. Grouping by a *derived* value (not a raw column) is also a small but important leap — it shows GROUP BY works on expressions, not just columns.

## How to read YoY
Once you have revenue per year, year-over-year growth is just each year compared to the one above it. Even reading the rows top to bottom tells you the direction; the exact % is the next refinement.

weeks.title: Statistical thinking for analysts
weeks.context:
Everything you found in weeks 1 through 5 is a pattern. Patterns are not findings. A finding is a pattern with evidence that it is real and not noise. "Furniture margins are lower than Technology margins" is a pattern. "Furniture margins are 7.2 percentage points lower than Technology margins (95% CI: 5.8 to 8.6 pp, p < 0.001)" is a finding you can defend.

Most business analysts never learn this distinction formally, which means most business analyses are underpowered. Someone presents "the West region grew 4% faster than the East" without asking whether 4% is a real difference or whether it would disappear with a different time window. Statisticians call this the file-drawer problem -- the analyses that do not show a significant result get quietly put away, and the ones that show a positive result get presented, regardless of how noisy the signal is.

This week you upgrade every finding from weeks 1 through 5 with appropriate statistical support. Confidence intervals around mean profit margin by Category. A t-test comparing VIP customer order values to Low Value customer order values. The Pearson correlation between Discount and Profit with a p-value. And a check for Simpson's paradox -- whether an aggregate finding reverses when you break it down by a subgroup.

Simpson's paradox is worth a specific example. If Technology has the best overall margin but the worst margin in the West region, the aggregate finding is misleading for the West region sales team. Any recommendation based on "Technology is our best category" could lead the West team to push the exact subcategory where they are losing money. Checking for reversal is not optional when regional or segment breakdowns exist.

By Sunday: every key finding in the Superstore analysis upgraded with a confidence interval or p-value, Simpson's paradox check documented for at least one finding, and the analyst memo updated to reflect the statistical framing.

days.title: Samples and selection bias

items.title: Samples and selection bias
items.body:
## What it is
Your data is almost always a **sample**, not the whole population. **Selection bias** is when that sample isn't representative — so a pattern in it may say more about *who got into the data* than about reality.

## Why it matters
"Patterns are not findings." A finding is a pattern with evidence it's real *and* generalisable. If the sample is skewed, even a strong, statistically clean pattern can be an artefact. Three common forms quietly distort analysis:

- **Survivorship bias** — you see the customers who checked out, not the carts abandoned. Conclusions about "what customers want" miss everyone who left.
- **Self-selection** — people who leave reviews are systematically happier or angrier than the silent majority.
- **Coverage** — Superstore is *one* retailer's orders. Patterns here ("Tables lose money") may not hold for retail in general.

## The habit
Before trusting any pattern, ask: *who or what is missing from this data, and would including them change the story?* This question costs ten seconds and saves you from confidently shipping a conclusion your sample never supported.

Read it as a *coverage check*, not a result: this is **4 years, one company, US-only, South under-represented**. So any claim you make is really "for this retailer, 2014-17, mostly West/East." That scoping isn't pedantry — it's the difference between an honest finding and an overclaim. Bias isn't fixed by more rows; it's fixed by representativeness, which a count like this helps you see.

items.title: Confidence intervals
items.body:
## What it is
A single number — "average margin = 7.2%" — hides uncertainty. A **confidence interval (CI)** gives a *range* that probably contains the true value (95% is the usual level). The less data you have, the wider that range.

## Why it matters
"Margins are 7.2% lower" sounds exact and authoritative. "7.2% lower, 95% CI [3.1%, 11.3%]" is *honest* — and far more useful, because it tells the reader how much to trust the estimate. The killer application: if you're comparing two groups and the CI of their *difference* crosses zero, you cannot claim there's a real difference at all. CIs are how you avoid betting the business on noise.

## The intuition
A CI is built from the **standard error** — roughly, how much your sample average would wobble if you'd drawn a different sample. More data shrinks the standard error, so the interval tightens. A wide CI is the data honestly telling you "I'm not sure".

items.title: Deeper dive: Confidence intervals

items.title: See it in code (with output)
items.body:
## Compute a 95% CI for a sub-category's profit
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```python
import numpy as np
x = df.loc[df["Sub-Category"] == "Tables", "Profit"]

mean = x.mean()
se   = x.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(x))      # standard error
lo, hi = mean - 1.96*se, mean + 1.96*se
print(f"n={len(x)}  mean={mean:.1f}  95% CI = [{lo:.1f}, {hi:.1f}]")
```
Output (illustrative):
```
n=319  mean=-55.6  95% CI = [-76.2, -35.0]
```
Read it: Tables average a **loss** of ~$56/order, and the whole interval is **below zero** — so "Tables are unprofitable on average" is a claim the data genuinely supports, not noise. If the interval had been, say, [-20, +15], you couldn't say that.
```python
# A wider interval from a tiny group honestly says 'not sure'
small = df[df["Sub-Category"]=="Copiers"]["Profit"]
print(len(small))   # ~68 -> wider CI than Tables
```

items.title: Correlation
items.body:
## What it is
**Correlation (r)** measures how strongly two numeric variables move together, on a fixed scale from **-1 to +1**: +1 a perfect upward line, -1 a perfect downward line, 0 no linear relationship. The **sign** is the direction; the **magnitude** is the strength.

## Why it matters
In Week 3 you *eyeballed* discount vs profit on a scatter. Correlation replaces "they look related" with "r = -0.22, a weak-to-moderate negative relationship" — a single, comparable, defensible number. You can compute it across many pairs at once to see which relationships are worth investigating, turning a wall of columns into a ranked shortlist.

## How to read |r|
Roughly: |r| above ~0.7 is strong, ~0.3-0.7 moderate, below ~0.3 weak. But always pair r with a scatter — r only captures *linear* relationships, so a strong curved relationship can show a near-zero r. The number and the picture together tell the truth; either alone can fool you.

days.title: Correlation is not causation
days.summary: Concept, video, then a confounder worked through. Always ask 'what else explains this?'

items.title: Correlation is not causation
items.body:
## What it is
Two variables moving together doesn't mean one **causes** the other. Very often a hidden third variable — a **confounder** — drives both, manufacturing a correlation between things that have no direct link.

## Why it matters
Your Week 3 finding ("high discounts -> losses") is *correlational*. Two stories fit the same data: (a) discounts directly cause losses, or (b) clearance items that were *already* low-margin happen to get the deepest discounts — so the low margin causes both the discount *and* the loss. Same correlation, completely different action: (a) says "cap discounts"; (b) says "stop stocking those items". Asking "what else could explain this?" is the single habit that separates an analyst from a chart-generator.

## The classic to remember
Ice-cream sales correlate with shark attacks. Neither causes the other; the confounder is **summer** (hot weather drives both). Whenever you see a striking correlation, hunt for the summer.

```
Bookcases   0.211
Appliances  0.166
```
The loss-leaders (Binders, Machines, Tables) also carry the **deepest average discounts** — so discount and "troubled sub-category" are tangled together. That doesn't kill your finding, but it means the honest claim is "discounts are *associated* with losses" until you isolate the effect (e.g. compare profit at the same discount level *within* one sub-category). Stating it as "discounts *cause* losses" would be overreach — and a sharp stakeholder would catch it.

cards.whenRight: Correct — association is not causation; a confounder can drive both.
cards.whenWrong: It doesn't — correlation never proves cause on its own.

cards.prompt: A confounder is a hidden variable that influences both correlated variables.
cards.whenRight: Right — it creates the correlation without either causing the other.
cards.whenWrong: It is — a confounder drives both, faking a direct link.

days.title: Is the difference real? (hypothesis testing)
days.summary: Concept, then a t-test printed. A p-value separates signal from noise.

items.title: Is the difference real? (hypothesis testing)
items.body:
## What it is
"Furniture margin < Technology margin" — real difference, or just random wobble in this sample? A **hypothesis test** (here a t-test) returns a **p-value**: the probability of seeing a gap *this big* if there were truly *no* difference between the groups.

## Why it matters
Without it, you over-read every wiggle. A small p-value (commonly < 0.05) means "this gap would be rare if nothing were going on" — so it's likely real and worth acting on. A large p-value means you simply don't have enough evidence yet. This is the tool that stops you from building a recommendation on a difference that's actually noise — exactly the credibility a stakeholder is paying for.

## The one misreading to avoid
A big p-value does **not** prove "no difference" — it proves "insufficient evidence to claim one". Absence of proof isn't proof of absence. And a tiny p-value on a tiny, meaningless difference is statistically significant but practically irrelevant — always check the *size* of the effect too, not just the p-value.

items.title: Deeper dive: Is the difference real? (hypothesis testing)
items.body:
## Deeper dive: Is the difference real? (hypothesis testing)

There isn't a single short video that nails this exact concept, so work it the way professionals actually learn it — by running small variations yourself and reading the output.

## Two more worked examples
1. Take the smallest case of **Is the difference real? (hypothesis testing)** and predict the result *before* you run it. Then run it and compare — the gap between your prediction and reality is the learning.
2. Change one variable (a column, a parameter, a condition) and predict again. Repeat until your predictions are reliably right.

## What to watch for
- Trace the data through each step (split, apply, combine) rather than memorising syntax.
- Read the shape and the index of every intermediate result; most bugs are shape bugs.
- When stuck, shrink the input to 3 rows you can verify by hand.

items.title: See it in code (with output)
items.body:
## t-test: Furniture vs Technology profit
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```python
from scipy import stats
furn = df.loc[df["Category"]=="Furniture",  "Profit"]
tech = df.loc[df["Category"]=="Technology", "Profit"]

t, p = stats.ttest_ind(furn, tech, equal_var=False)
print(f"Furniture mean={furn.mean():.1f}, Technology mean={tech.mean():.1f}")
print(f"t={t:.2f}, p={p:.4f}")
```
Output (illustrative):
```
Furniture mean=8.7, Technology mean=78.8
t=-7.31, p=0.0000
```
Read it: Technology orders are far more profitable on average, and **p < 0.0001** says a gap that large would essentially never happen by chance — so the difference is real, not noise. Now you can write "Technology is significantly more profitable than Furniture (p<0.001)" and defend it. Had p been 0.4, the honest statement would be "no significant difference detected".

cards.prompt: A small p-value (e.g. < 0.05) suggests the observed difference is unlikely to be just noise.
cards.whenRight: Right — low p = the gap would be rare if there were truly no difference.
cards.whenWrong: It does — a small p-value is evidence the difference is real.
cards.sim: p=0.0000 -> difference is real, not chance

cards.prompt: A p-value above 0.05 proves there is no difference between the groups.
cards.whenRight: Correct — it means insufficient evidence, not proof of 'no difference'.
cards.whenWrong: Not proof — high p means you can't conclude a difference, not that none exists.

days.title: Simpson's paradox
days.summary: Concept, video, then the reversal shown in code. Always check the subgroups.

items.title: Simpson's paradox
items.body:
## What it is
**Simpson's paradox**: a trend that appears in aggregated data can **disappear or reverse** when you split into subgroups (and vice versa). The whole tells one story; the parts tell the opposite.

## Why it matters
It's not a curiosity — it's a trap you can fall into every week. "Discounts barely dent profit on average" can be flatly wrong once you split by category, exactly as you saw in Week 3 Day 4: the blended average looked survivable while Furniture was haemorrhaging money and Technology shrugged it off. The aggregate *lied*; the subgroups told the truth. This is the deep reason you always break down before you conclude — and why an aggregate number should make you ask "is this hiding opposite subgroups?"

## How to defend against it
Whenever you report an aggregate, split it by the most relevant dimension (category, region, segment) and check the trend still holds. If a subgroup reverses it, the subgroup is usually the real story.

weeks.title: AI-Augmented analyst + Prompt Engineering
weeks.context:
Every analyst you will compete with for jobs has access to Claude, ChatGPT, and Copilot. The ones who use AI well will be more productive. The ones who use it carelessly will produce confident-sounding wrong answers that are embarrassing to defend. This week you learn to be the first kind.

The discipline is verification. AI is genuinely excellent at generating SQL, writing formula syntax, drafting memo templates, and suggesting chart types. It is unreliable at interpreting data it cannot see, making business judgements that require domain knowledge, and catching subtle errors in analysis. Knowing which tasks to outsource and which to keep is the skill -- and it is a skill you practise by deliberately testing AI outputs against your own analysis this week.

The specific workflows you will build: a schema-aware SQL prompt (you paste the CREATE TABLE statement plus a question, AI generates the query, you run it and verify the output), a memo draft-and-critique loop (you paste your findings in bullet points, AI drafts a memo, you edit for accuracy and voice), and a formula generation prompt (you describe the logic in plain English, AI generates the Excel formula, you verify with spot checks).

The prompts.md file is the deliverable. Not the analysis -- you have already done the analysis. The deliverable is a documented set of prompts that work reliably for your analytical workflow, with notes on what each prompt is good for and where it fails. This is your personal AI cheatsheet, and it compounds over time: the better you get at prompting for analysis tasks, the more you can outsource the mechanical parts and spend your time on the parts that require actual thinking.

By Sunday: prompts.md committed to the Superstore repo with at least five working prompts, each with a "use for / not for" annotation, and one documented example where AI produced a wrong answer and you caught it.

items.title: AI accelerates, you stay accountable
items.body:
## What it is
Every analyst you'll compete with has Claude, ChatGPT, and Copilot. The edge isn't *using* AI — it's using it **well**: let it draft, then **you verify against the data**, and you remain accountable for every number you ship.

## Why it matters
AI is fluent, and fluency reads as confidence — but fluency is not accuracy. It will write a plausible SQL query against columns that don't exist, or invent a statistic, in the same self-assured tone it uses when it's right. Ship that unchecked and you'll be humiliated defending a wrong number in a meeting. Used with verification, the same tool makes you 2-3x faster with *no* loss of trust. The whole skill this week is building the verify-reflex so AI's speed never becomes AI's risk.

## The contract
AI supplies *drafts and syntax*; you supply *the data, the judgement, and the final sign-off*. It never gets to be the source of a number — only a faster way to produce something you then check.

items.title: Schema-aware prompts for SQL
items.body:
## What it is
AI writes SQL fast — but only well if you hand it the **table schema** (columns + types) and a **precise question**. A vague prompt yields a confident, plausible, *wrong* query (joining columns that don't exist, mislabelling aggregates).

## Why it matters
You already wrote these exact queries by hand in Week 5, which makes this the perfect, safe place to learn prompting: you can *verify* the AI against an answer you trust. The lesson generalises — on real jobs you'll prompt against schemas you know, paste the result, and check it. Schema-aware prompting is the difference between AI as a force-multiplier and AI as a generator of subtle bugs.

## The pattern
Always give it: the table name, the columns (with types if it matters), and the exact output you want. Then **run** the SQL it returns and compare to a known result before you trust it.

## Weak vs strong prompt
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```text
WEAK:   "write SQL to find my best products"
        -> AI guesses column names; likely wrong.

STRONG: "Table superstore(order_id, sub_category, category, sales, profit,
         discount, order_date, customer_name). Write SQLite returning each
         sub_category's total profit, highest first."
```
AI returns:
```sql
SELECT sub_category, SUM(profit) AS total_profit
FROM superstore GROUP BY sub_category ORDER BY total_profit DESC;
```
Now **verify** — run it and compare to your Week 5 hand-written answer:
```
sub_category  total_profit
Copiers        55617.8
Phones         44515.7
Accessories    41936.6
```
Matches Week 5 exactly -> trust it. If it hadn't matched, the prompt or the query was wrong, and you'd have caught it *because you checked*.

items.title: AI as a memo drafter
items.body:
## What it is
Hand the AI **your** findings (the real numbers) plus the audience, and it drafts the memo prose in seconds. You then edit for accuracy, voice, and truth.

## Why it matters
Writing is the slow part of analysis; drafting from known points is where AI genuinely shines. But there's a hard rule: it must build *only* from numbers you supply. The instant you let it invent a figure to make a sentence flow, you've planted a landmine — invented numbers are how analysts get fired. So you feed it facts, it returns phrasing, and you delete anything you can't trace back to your own analysis.

## The pattern
Give it: the audience (and their technical level), your bullet findings *with numbers*, and the structure you want (headline -> evidence -> recommendation, word limit). Then edit ruthlessly — for your voice and to strip any claim the data doesn't back.

```text
- AI wrote "discounts have devastated margins for years" -> DELETE (no time-series claim in your data)
- AI wrote "~20% cap" -> KEEP (matches your tipping point)
```

days.title: Make AI critique your memo

items.title: Make AI critique your memo
items.body:
## What it is
Flip the tool from author to adversary: paste your finished memo and ask the AI to **attack it** — find unsupported claims, missing caveats, and alternative explanations a sharp reader would raise.

## Why it matters
You are blind to your own gaps because you know the context the reader doesn't. An adversarial pass *before* your boss sees it catches the embarrassing holes while they're still cheap to fix — the correlation-stated-as-causation, the claim with no number, the recommendation with no cost. It's like having a skeptical senior analyst on call, for free, who never gets tired or political. You stay in control: you decide which critiques are fair and act on those.

## The pattern
Cast the AI in a demanding role ("skeptical data director"), ask for a *specific* number of weaknesses and the questions you'd get grilled on. Specific roles and counts produce sharper critique than "what do you think?".

```text
"You are a skeptical data director. Find the 3 weakest claims in this memo
```

items.title: AI for slide content
items.body:
## What it is
Give the AI your memo and ask for **slide bullets and speaker notes**. It compresses prose into talking points so you can *present*, not read aloud.

## Why it matters
Executives get a deck, not a notebook, and the hardest part of a deck is brutal compression — saying the finding in five words on the slide and two sentences out loud. AI is fast at that first pass; your job is to cut further, because the failure mode of AI slides is *too many* words. A lean slide with strong speaker notes is how a finding actually lands in the room, and AI gets you to a draft deck in a minute instead of an hour.

## The pattern
Ask for a fixed, small structure: N slides, each with a short title, ≤3 brief bullets, and 2 sentences of speaker notes. Then trim every bullet that isn't essential — slides are signposts, the notes carry the detail.

items.title: AI for tricky formulas and code
items.body:
## What it is
Stuck on a gnarly Excel formula or a pandas one-liner? Describe what you want in plain English; the AI writes it. Then **test it on a case where you already know the answer**.

## Why it matters
This removes the syntax bottleneck — the 20 minutes lost to "how do I do a year-over-year % in pandas again?" — and lets you stay in the flow of the analysis. But an unverified formula silently produces a wrong column that poisons everything downstream, and you won't see the error because the code *ran*. The verify-on-a-known-case habit is the cheap insurance that keeps AI's speed from quietly corrupting your results.

## The pattern
Describe the calculation and the columns; get the formula; apply it; then hand-check one row you can compute yourself. If that row matches, trust it across the data. If it doesn't, you caught a bug for the price of one mental subtraction.

```
   year   revenue  yoy_pct
0  2014  484247.5      NaN
```

weeks.title: Superstore v0.5: Executive deck
weeks.context:
You have five weeks of Superstore analysis. Now you compress it into five slides that a CEO can read in 10 minutes and act on. That compression is harder than the analysis.

The instinct when building an executive deck is to show everything you found, arranged roughly in the order you found it. This instinct produces a 20-slide deck where the recommendation is on slide 19. By slide 15, the CEO has moved on to email. An executive deck starts with the answer, then uses the subsequent slides as evidence. This is the Pyramid Principle: conclusion first, then the three or four arguments that support it, then the data that supports each argument.

Each slide has one headline. Not a title that says what the slide is about ("Profitability Analysis"), but a headline that states the finding ("Furniture margins are 7.2 pp below Technology, driven by discounts above 20%"). The difference matters because the title deck requires the reader to derive the insight from the chart; the headline deck gives them the insight and uses the chart as proof. Senior audiences -- the kind who review 15 decks a week -- always prefer the headline deck.

The five slides are: (1) the overall situation and recommendation, (2) the profitability finding, (3) the discount finding, (4) the customer segmentation finding, (5) the three specific recommended actions with estimated impact. Slide 5 is the most important slide in the deck. A deck that ends on "here are the findings" is an analysis report dressed as a deck. A deck that ends on "here are three specific actions and here is what they will change" is a business case.

By Sunday: a five-slide deck in Google Slides or PowerPoint, exported as PDF and committed to the repo, and a rehearsed two-minute version you can deliver from memory.

items.title: The deck is an argument, not a dump
items.body:
## What it is
An executive deck is not your notebook with borders. It is a **10-minute argument** aimed at a busy decision-maker: lead with the answer, make one point per slide, and end on an action they can approve.

## Why it matters
The instinct after five weeks of work is to *show the work* — every chart, every caveat. That instinct buries the point and exhausts the reader. Executives reward **clarity, not completeness**: they will act on five slides they understood and ignore twenty they didn't. Compression is genuinely harder than the analysis — it forces you to decide what actually matters — which is exactly why it's the skill that separates analysts who influence decisions from those who just produce reports nobody reads.

## The shape of a winning deck
Five slides: (1) headline + recommendation, (2-4) one finding each with its single best chart, (5) the recommendation with expected impact and next step. Everything that doesn't serve the decision gets cut, not shrunk. The deck is a spine; your voice carries the rest.

items.title: Slide 1 — the headline (BLUF)
items.body:
## What it is
**BLUF — Bottom Line Up Front.** Slide 1 states your single most important conclusion *and* the recommended action, in one sentence, *before* any evidence.

## Why it matters
Assume the reader sees only slide 1 — because often they will, or they'll decide in the first 20 seconds whether to keep paying attention. If the conclusion is buried on slide 12, you've lost. Leading with the answer also disciplines *you*: if you can't state the recommendation in one sentence with a number, you don't yet know what you're recommending. The headline is both the reader's shortcut and your own clarity test.

## What makes a strong headline
It's a *claim with a number and an implied action*, not a topic label. "Superstore Discount Analysis" is a filing-cabinet label. "Capping discounts at 30% would recover ~$62k in annual profit" tells the reader the stakes, the action, and the size — in nine words.

items.title: Slides 2-4 — one finding per slide
items.body:
## What it is
Your three evidence slides each carry **one** finding: the **claim as the slide title** (a full sentence), **one chart** that proves it, and **one line** of takeaway. One idea per slide, full stop.

## Why it matters
A slide with three ideas communicates none — the audience reads ahead, half-listens, and remembers nothing. Forcing one claim per slide does two things: it makes *you* decide what the finding actually is (a sentence, not a chart), and it lets the audience follow your argument one clean step at a time. The title carrying the claim is the trick most analysts miss: a title like "Discounts" makes the reader work out the point; "Discounts above 30% turn orders unprofitable" hands it to them.

## The discipline
Title = the claim. Body = the *single* best chart that proves it (not three related ones). Footer = one sentence of "so what". If you have a second chart you love, it goes in an appendix, not the slide.

items.title: Slide 5 — the recommendation
items.body:
## What it is
The final slide answers the only question the executive truly has: **"so what do we do?"** — a concrete action, its expected impact, and the immediate next step.

## Why it matters
Findings without a recommendation make the audience do *your* job — and they won't; they'll table it. The recommendation is the entire reason the analysis existed, and it's what gets remembered and acted on after everyone leaves the room. A vague "we should consider optimising discounts" wastes the build-up; a specific, quantified, time-bound action ("cap at 30%, ~$62k upside, pilot one region next quarter") is something a leader can say yes to on the spot.

## What it must contain
Three things: the **action** (specific enough to execute), the **expected impact** (a number — the prize), and the **next step** (a small, low-risk move like a pilot). Specific, quantified, actionable — never hedged.

days.title: Design pass — make it credible
days.summary: Consistency and decluttering. Concept + a concrete checklist.

items.title: Design pass — make it credible
items.body:
## What it is
A pass purely for **visual consistency** and **decluttering**: identical title styling on every slide, one colour per category used everywhere, aligned elements, labelled axes — and ruthless removal of "chartjunk" (3D effects, gradients, gridlines and borders that carry no information).

## Why it matters
Design is a credibility signal whether you like it or not. If the deck looks sloppy — mismatched fonts, a category that's blue here and orange there, an unlabelled axis — the audience quietly distrusts the *analysis* behind it, even if the numbers are flawless. Clean, consistent design borrows trust for your conclusions; messy design taxes them. It's the cheapest credibility you'll ever buy, and most analysts skip it.

## The standard
Pick one rule per element and apply it everywhere. Same title font and size. Furniture is *always* the same colour. Every axis labelled. Every chart has a takeaway. Nothing on a slide that doesn't earn its place.

items.title: Deeper dive: Design pass — make it credible
items.body:
## Deeper dive: Design pass — make it credible

There isn't a single short video that nails this exact concept, so work it the way professionals actually learn it — by running small variations yourself and reading the output.

## Two more worked examples
1. Take the smallest case of **Design pass — make it credible** and predict the result *before* you run it. Then run it and compare — the gap between your prediction and reality is the learning.
2. Change one variable (a column, a parameter, a condition) and predict again. Repeat until your predictions are reliably right.

## What to watch for
- Trace the data through each step (split, apply, combine) rather than memorising syntax.
- Read the shape and the index of every intermediate result; most bugs are shape bugs.
- When stuck, shrink the input to 3 rows you can verify by hand.

items.title: See it worked (the checklist)
items.body:
## Run this checklist over every slide
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```text
[ ] Titles: same font, size, position on all slides
[ ] Colour: each category ONE consistent colour across every chart
[ ] Axes: labelled, with units; no mystery numbers
[ ] Clutter: no 3D, no gradients, no decorative gridlines/borders
[ ] Numbers: rounded sensibly (62k, not 61,847.39)
[ ] One takeaway line per chart slide
[ ] Alignment: titles and charts line up slide to slide
```
Before vs after this pass is the difference between "a student made this" and "I trust this person with a decision".

days.title: Rehearse the 5-minute pitch
days.summary: Delivery sells the analysis. Concept + a self-review rubric.

items.title: Rehearse the 5-minute pitch
items.body:
## What it is
Practise delivering the deck in **5 minutes** — headline, three findings, recommendation — and **record yourself once**, then watch it back.

## Why it matters
The best analysis in the world loses the room if the delivery is shaky, rushed, or hedged. Recording is uncomfortable and exactly why it works: it surfaces the filler words, the slides you can't actually explain, and the moments you go over time — all while it's still cheap to fix, in private, instead of in front of your boss. Five minutes is a deliberate constraint; if you can't make the case in five, you haven't found the core yet.

## What to watch for
Filler ("um", "kind of", "I think maybe") that signals low confidence; any slide you couldn't explain in one breath (it's too complex — simplify it); and overruns (the fix is to *cut content*, never to talk faster).

weeks.title: Superstore v1.0: Ship + retro
weeks.context:
The Superstore project has been running for eight weeks. The memo is two pages, the deck is five slides, the dashboard is one sheet, queries.sql has eight queries, monthly_report.py runs in five minutes, and the GitHub repo has everything committed. This week you finish it -- properly.

"Properly" means three things. First, you get one outside reader to look at the memo or the deck and tell you what confused them. Not a friend who will tell you it looks great -- someone who will actually use it. Second, you write a project retrospective. Third, you anonymise the data for sharing and update the repo README to reflect the final state.

The outside reader is not optional. The analyst's curse is that you know what every chart means because you built it. A reader who did not build it will find the one label you forgot, the one chart that has no axis title, and the one recommendation that is not specific enough. Every team you will join as a working analyst has a "two-eyes" rule for deliverables: no analysis leaves the team without another pair of eyes. You are practising that discipline now.

The retrospective is a one-page honest document, not a celebration. Three questions: what took longer than you expected, what would you do differently if you started over, and what is the single most useful thing you learned. The answers to these questions are the learning you take into Project 2. Skipping the retrospective means carrying the same blind spots into the next project.

The Superstore dataset is fictional and does not require anonymisation, but the practice of scrubbing a dataset before sharing is good professional hygiene. Replace "Customer Name" with "Customer ID" (it already exists), confirm no personal information made it into the analysis files, and note the data source and licence in the README.

By Sunday: outside reader feedback documented in the repo, RETRO.md committed, dataset anonymisation confirmed, and the README updated to reflect the final project state with links to all four deliverables.

items.title: Find the rough edges
items.body:
## What it is
Before the final ship, audit every artefact — notebook, memo, deck, dashboard, `queries.sql`, repo README — and write down every **rough edge**: half-finished bits, inconsistencies, broken links, unclear labels, numbers that disagree across documents.

## Why it matters
"Shipping" means *finishing*, not *abandoning*, and "it's basically done" is where most portfolio projects quietly die at 80%. A written rough-edge list converts that vague feeling into a concrete, completable punch list — and the act of hunting for edges always finds the embarrassing one (the figure that's $62k in the memo and $61k on the deck) that would have cost you credibility. You can't fix what you haven't named.

## How to audit
Open each artefact as if you were a stranger reviewing it for a job. Note everything that's wrong, unclear, or inconsistent — don't fix yet, just list. A good audit usually finds 5-10 items you'd otherwise have shipped.

items.body:
## What it is
Move the memo out of raw markdown into a properly formatted document — clear heading hierarchy, one readable body font, embedded charts at sensible sizes, page numbers, maybe a simple header with your name and date.

## Why it matters
A non-technical reader judges credibility partly by *format*, before they read a word. The identical content reads as more authoritative in a clean PDF than in a plain `.md` file — fair or not, that's how decision-makers respond. On real jobs the deliverable is almost always a polished doc or slides, never a markdown file, so building the habit now matters. Format is the wrapper that makes good content get taken seriously.

## The spec
H1 title, H2 section headings (Headline / Evidence / Recommendation), one body font, charts embedded inline with captions, page numbers, your name + date. One page if you can.

## What it is
Create a version you can show the world. Superstore is a public sample dataset, so confirm there's nothing private (no real PII, no credentials, no internal-only commentary) before it goes on your public GitHub and portfolio.

## Why it matters
You *want* recruiters to find and read this — that's the point of a portfolio. A public-safe pass lets you share freely without ever leaking something you shouldn't, and it builds the exact habit that matters far more on real company projects later, where an accidental key or customer record in a public repo is a fireable, sometimes legal, problem. Practising "scrub before public" on safe data now means you won't slip on dangerous data later.

Confirm the dataset is the public sample; remove internal TODOs and private notes from the notebook; ensure no API keys, credentials, or absolute file paths are committed; gitignore the raw data if licensing requires it.

days.title: Get one real reader

items.title: Get one real reader
items.body:
## What it is
Give your memo or deck to **one person who hasn't seen the project** and watch (or ask) where they slow down, re-read, or get confused.

## Why it matters
You are constitutionally blind to your own clarity gaps — you know too much, so the jargon, the unexplained jump, and the chart with no takeaway are invisible to *you* but obvious to a fresh reader. This is the single cheapest, highest-impact quality boost available: five minutes with one outsider finds more real problems than an hour of you re-reading your own work, because you'll only ever read it as the person who already understands it.

## The killer test
Ask them: "Read this, then tell me in one sentence what I'm recommending and why." If they can't, your headline and structure aren't doing their job — and you've found that out for free, before it mattered.

items.body:
## The one-question reader test
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```text
YOU:    "Read this memo, then tell me in one sentence what I'm recommending
         and why."
READER: "Um... that discounts are bad? And maybe cap them somewhere?"
        ^ if this is vague, your headline failed -> fix slide 1 / the headline

WATCH FOR (note every one):
  - where they re-read a sentence (it's unclear)
  - a term they pause on (undefined jargon)
  - a chart they skip (no takeaway, or too busy)
  - "wait, which number?" (inconsistent figures)
```
Their confusion is your punch list for tomorrow.

days.title: Fix what confused them
days.summary: Reader confusion is data. Fix the work, don't defend it. Concept + worked fixes.

items.title: Fix what confused them
items.body:
## What it is
Turn your reader's confusion into a fix list and apply it: define the jargon, add the missing context, label the chart, tighten the headline, reconcile the number.

## Why it matters
The instinct is to *explain* — "well, what they didn't understand is..." — and you must kill it, because in the real meeting you won't be standing next to every reader to clarify. If one fresh reader was confused, the artefact is unclear, and the next reader (your boss, a recruiter) will be confused too, except they won't tell you — they'll just move on. Treating confusion as a defect in the *work* rather than the *reader* is the mindset that produces things people actually understand. Clarity beats cleverness every time.

## The rule
Every point of confusion becomes a concrete edit. You don't have to act on *opinions* ("I'd use a different colour"), but you must act on *confusion* ("I didn't get what this chart shows").

Notice you're fixing the *work*, never arguing with the reader. That's the whole discipline.

weeks.title: Project 2 — HR Attrition v0.1
weeks.context:
The Superstore project was a retailer. This week you start a very different domain: human resources. The IBM HR Analytics dataset contains 1,470 employees with 35 columns covering age, gender, department, job role, salary, overtime hours, tenure, satisfaction scores, and most importantly a binary column called Attrition (Yes/No) indicating whether each employee left the company.

Employee attrition costs money. A mid-level engineer who leaves costs roughly 150% of their annual salary to replace -- recruiting fees, onboarding time, lost productivity during the vacancy. For a department with 200 engineers where 15% leave per year, that is $4.5 million annually assuming $200K salaries. An analysis that identifies which employees are at highest risk of leaving -- and what predictors are associated with that risk -- can prioritise interventions that cost a fraction of that.

Your job this week is not to build a prediction model. It is to build four pivot tables, each answering a specific question about which sub-population has the highest attrition rate. The four questions: which departments have the highest attrition rates, which job roles have the highest rates, which salary bands have the highest rates, and how does overtime status interact with attrition? The answers will be specific numbers, not observations about "elevated risk."

Attrition rate is computed as: (employees who left) / (total employees in that group). In the dataset, this means counting the "Yes" values in the Attrition column divided by the total count for each group. COUNTIFS handles this directly. The denominator is total employees in the group, not total employees in the company.

By Sunday: a new GitHub repo named hr-attrition-analysis with the IBM dataset, four pivot tables with attrition rates computed correctly, and a README stating the two highest-risk combinations you found.

concept_check.q: Compute the attrition rate by Department using COUNTIFS: =COUNTIFS(Department_col, department, Attrition_col, "Yes") / COUNTIFS(Department_col, department, Attrition_col, "*"). Paste the table: Depart?
concept_check.explain: See the lesson for explanation. The right answer follows directly from the core idea taught today.

concept_check.q: Build the Job Role attrition table. Paste all 9 job roles ranked by attrition rate. Write one sentence about the two job roles at the top and what they have in common (compensation level, manager-to-I?
concept_check.explain: See the lesson for explanation. The right answer follows directly from the core idea taught today.

concept_check.q: Bucket MonthlyIncome into salary bands ($0-3K, $3K-6K, $6K-9K, $9K+) using nested IF. Compute attrition rate by band. Paste the table. Does attrition decrease monotonically with salary? If not -- if t?
concept_check.explain: See the lesson for explanation. The right answer follows directly from the core idea taught today.

items.title: Why people analytics
items.body:
## What it is
Last project you analysed a retailer; now you turn the same rigour on **people**. **Attrition** is employees leaving the company, and **people analytics** is using data to understand who leaves and why — instead of guessing.

## Why it matters
Attrition is brutally expensive: replacing an employee costs roughly **50-200% of their annual salary** (recruiting, onboarding, lost productivity). HR decisions are too often made on gut feel — "people leave for money" — when the data frequently says something else entirely (overtime, no promotion, a specific role). Finding the *real* drivers lets a company spend its retention budget where it actually moves the needle. This is exactly the analytical thinking from Project 1, applied to a domain where one good finding can save millions.

## The dataset
The **IBM HR Analytics** dataset: 1,470 employees, 35 columns (age, department, job role, monthly income, overtime, years at company, years since promotion…). The target column is **Attrition** (`Yes`/`No`) — whether each employee left. Everything this week predicts or explains that one column.

items.title: See it in code (with output)
items.body:
## Load and find the base rate
The first question in any attrition study: what fraction actually left?
```python
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("HR-Employee-Attrition.csv")
print(df.shape)
print(df["Attrition"].value_counts())
print(df["Attrition"].value_counts(normalize=True).round(3))
```
Output:
```
(1470, 35)
No     1233
Yes     237
Name: Attrition, dtype: int64
No     0.839
Yes    0.161
Name: Attrition, dtype: float64
```
Read it: **16.1% of employees left** — that's your *base rate*, the number every group you analyse this week gets compared against. A department at 25% is a problem; one at 8% is a model. Note too that the classes are **imbalanced** (most stayed) — important to remember so you don't over-read small groups.

cards.prompt: The attrition rate is the share of employees whose Attrition is 'Yes' — a boolean mean.
cards.whenRight: Right — (Attrition=='Yes').mean() gives the rate, like the repeat-rate trick.
cards.whenWrong: It is — it's the proportion of 'Yes', exactly a boolean mean.

cards.prompt: Every department will have the same attrition rate as the 16% overall.
cards.whenRight: Correct — the whole project is finding which groups deviate from that base rate.
cards.whenWrong: Not so — groups vary widely; finding the deviations is the point.

items.title: Load and inspect
items.body:
## What it is
Same discipline as every dataset: before analysing, **look**. `head`, `info`, `describe`, and the target's balance. With 35 columns you especially need to know what's numeric, what's categorical, and whether anything's missing.

## Why it matters
You can't analyse drivers of attrition until you know which columns *are* drivers (numeric like MonthlyIncome, categorical like Department) and that the data is clean. Inspecting also re-surfaces the **class imbalance** (only 16% left) — which matters because a group with just 10 employees can show a wild attrition rate that's pure noise. Knowing your column types now also tells you which technique each driver needs: `groupby` for categoricals, `pd.cut` then groupby for numerics.

## What to check
Column count and types (`info`), missing values (the IBM set is clean — confirm it), the spread of key numerics (`describe`), and the target balance again so it's front of mind.

## Inspect the structure
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```

Columns: 35 ...
```

## A reusable helper: encode the target as 0/1
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```python
df["left"] = (df["Attrition"] == "Yes").astype(int)
```

days.title: Attrition by department
days.summary: The core move: a rate per group. Concept, video, then department rates vs the base.

items.title: Attrition by department
items.body:
## What it is
The workhorse question: **which departments lose the most people?** Group by `Department`, take the mean of your 0/1 `left` column, and you get each department's attrition rate — directly comparable to the 16.1% base rate.

## Why it matters
"We have a turnover problem" is useless to act on; "Sales runs 20.6% attrition vs 13.8% in R&D" tells leadership exactly where to focus. Comparing each group to the base rate is the move that turns a single company-wide number into a *map* of where the problem actually lives. This is the same split-apply-combine you've used since Week 2 — now answering an expensive HR question.

## The pattern
`groupby` the category, `.mean()` the 0/1 target for the rate, and `.count()` (or size) alongside so you know each group is big enough to trust. Always sort, and always compare to the base rate.

## Attrition rate per department
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```python
dept = df.groupby("Department").agg(
    attrition_rate=("left", "mean"),
    employees=("left", "count"),
).sort_values("attrition_rate", ascending=False)
print(dept.round(3))
```
Output (illustrative):
```
                        attrition_rate  employees
Department
Sales                            0.206        446
Human Resources                  0.190         63
Research & Development           0.138        961
```
Read it against the 16.1% base: **Sales (20.6%) is well above** average and is the biggest group, so it's the priority. HR is high too but only 63 people, so treat that rate with some caution. R&D is below base — relatively healthy. One groupby just turned "we have turnover" into "Sales is the problem".

## What it is
Department is coarse. Drill into **JobRole** — the same rate-per-group move, one level finer — to find the specific roles bleeding talent.

## Why it matters
A department average can hide a disaster in one role (a near-Simpson's effect you met in the stats week). Sales overall is 20.6%, but that blends calm roles with one that's on fire. Pinpointing the *role* lets HR target a fix — a specific role's pay, workload, or career path — instead of a vague "fix Sales". The finer the actionable unit, the more useful the finding.

Identical to yesterday, just group by `JobRole`. Sort, keep counts, and look for roles far above the base rate — those are your hotspots.

items.title: Does pay drive leaving?
items.body:
## What it is
Now a *numeric* driver: `MonthlyIncome`. You can't group by a continuous salary directly, so **bin it** with `pd.cut` into bands, then compute the attrition rate per band — exactly the cut-then-groupby move from the discount week.

## Why it matters
"People leave for money" is the most common HR assumption, and data lets you test it instead of repeating it. If attrition falls steeply as pay rises, comp is a real lever; if it's flat, the money story is a myth and you should look elsewhere (overtime, promotion). Either way you've replaced a belief with evidence — and possibly saved the company from throwing raises at a problem raises won't fix.

## The pattern
`pd.cut(MonthlyIncome, bins)` to create salary bands, then `groupby(band)["left"].mean()`. Watch the trend across bands top to bottom.

## Attrition rate by salary band
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```python
df["income_band"] = pd.cut(df["MonthlyIncome"],
    bins=[0, 3000, 6000, 10000, 20000],
    labels=["<3k", "3-6k", "6-10k", "10k+"])
```

items.title: The overtime effect
items.body:
## What it is
`OverTime` is a simple `Yes`/`No` column — so no binning needed, just compare the attrition rate for those who work overtime vs those who don't.

## Why it matters
Simple often wins. In the IBM data, overtime turns out to be one of the **single strongest** predictors of leaving — frequently a bigger effect than pay or role. That's a hugely actionable finding because overtime is a *managed* variable: a company can change workload policy far faster than it can restructure salaries. It's also a lesson in analytical humility — the most powerful driver is sometimes the plainest column, which you'd miss if you only chased the fancy ones.

## The pattern
A direct `groupby("OverTime")["left"].mean()`. Then quantify the gap (a ratio) — "overtime workers leave at Nx the rate" is the kind of crisp line that lands in a memo.

weeks.title: HR Attrition v0.2: Tenure + cohorts
weeks.context:
Last week you identified which departments and roles have the highest attrition rates. This week you add the time dimension: when in an employee's tenure is the attrition risk highest?

The tenure analysis is the question that converts "who leaves" into "when do they leave" -- which is what HR needs to design interventions. If attrition is highest in the first 12 months, the intervention is better onboarding and 30-60-90 day check-ins. If it is highest at the 2-3 year mark, the intervention is promotion pipeline clarity and salary reviews at that tenure point. If it is highest after 10+ years, the pattern is usually retirement-age exits or long-tenured employees who were not promoted and eventually stopped expecting to be.

The IBM dataset has YearsAtCompany and YearsInCurrentRole. You will bucket YearsAtCompany into tenure bands (0-1 years, 2-3, 4-5, 6-10, 10+) and compute attrition rate per band. The shape of the curve tells you where risk is concentrated. In most datasets, it is highest in the first two years. But some roles are different -- high-tenure technical specialists may show a late-career spike.

The promotion gap variable is worth engineering. Employees who have been in the same role longer than their peers -- defined as YearsInCurrentRole minus the median YearsInCurrentRole for their job role -- are more likely to feel stalled and leave. This is a feature, not a raw column; you have to compute it. The feature engineering is the analysis.

The 2D interaction cross-tab between tenure band and salary band (from week 10) is the most actionable finding this week. An employee in the 2-3 year tenure band who is also in the lowest salary band has a compounding risk that neither factor alone captures.

By Sunday: tenure band attrition table, promotion gap analysis, and the tenure × salary cross-tab all committed, with a one-paragraph summary of the "danger zone" combination.

days.title: What tenure analysis is
days.summary: From WHO leaves to WHEN they leave. Concept, then sketch the hypothesis.

items.title: What tenure analysis is
items.body:
## What it is
Last week you found *who* leaves (which departments, roles, pay levels). This week adds the **time dimension**: *when* in an employee's tenure is the risk highest? Tenure is `YearsAtCompany`, and the question is whether attrition risk is flat over time or spikes at certain points.

## Why it matters
The intervention changes completely depending on the answer. If risk spikes in the **first 1-2 years**, the problem is onboarding and early experience — fix the first 90 days. If it spikes around **years 3-5**, it's career stagnation — fix promotion and growth paths. A flat curve would mean tenure isn't the lever at all. You can't design a retention program until you know *when* people are at risk, and most companies have never actually looked.

## The discipline (again)
Form the hypothesis first, before plotting: most attrition research finds an **early-tenure spike** — new hires who realise it's not a fit and leave within two years. Write that prediction down, then test it.

## What it is

## Why it matters
This single table tests your hypothesis and usually delivers the project's most strategic insight: the **early-tenure spike**. items.title: Stagnation: years since promotion
items.body:
## What it is
`YearsSinceLastPromotion` measures career *stagnation* — how long since the employee last moved up. Group attrition rate by it (binned) to test whether being stuck drives people out.

## Why it matters
Stagnation is a distinct lever from tenure and pay. Someone can be well-paid and long-tenured but feel *stuck* — no promotion in five years — and that resentment is a classic exit trigger. If the data shows attrition climbing with the promotion gap, the fix isn't money, it's a visible growth path. Separating "stuck" from "underpaid" matters because the company would otherwise treat a career problem with a salary solution that won't work.

## The pattern
Same cut-then-groupby. Watch whether the rate rises as the promotion gap widens — and remember this is correlational (a confounder could lurk), so phrase findings as 'associated with'.

days.title: Plot a survival curve
days.summary: Visualise retention over tenure. Concept, video, then the cumulative-leave chart.

items.title: Plot a survival curve
items.body:
## What it is
A **survival curve** plots how the workforce thins out over tenure — the cumulative share still employed (or, flipped, the cumulative share who've left) by each year. It turns your tenure table into one intuitive picture.

## Why it matters
A curve communicates retention to non-analysts instantly in a way a table can't: a steep early drop *is* the early-tenure spike, visible at a glance. It's also the standard tool of professional people-analytics and medical statistics (where it's literally about survival), so producing one signals fluency. For your dashboard next week, this single chart can carry the whole tenure story.

## The pattern
Compute attrition rate per tenure year (or band), then plot it as a line; or compute the cumulative leave rate and plot that. Either way it's a `groupby` feeding a `matplotlib` line plot — Week 2's plotting skill on an HR question.

items.title: See it in code (with output)
items.body:
## Attrition rate by each tenure year, plotted
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
by_year = df.groupby("YearsAtCompany")["left"].mean()

by_year.plot(kind="line", marker="o", figsize=(9,5))
plt.axhline(df["left"].mean(), color="red", ls="--", label="base rate 16.1%")
plt.title("Attrition rate by years at company")
plt.xlabel("Years at company"); plt.ylabel("Attrition rate")
plt.legend(); plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig("attrition_by_tenure.png", dpi=150); plt.show()
```
The output is a line that starts **high on the left (year 0-1)** and falls toward and below the red base-rate line as tenure grows — the early-tenure spike, now a picture anyone can read. Describe it in your notebook: "risk is concentrated in the first two years, then drops below average." That sentence + this chart is dashboard-ready.

weeks.title: HR Attrition v0.3: Memo + dashboard
weeks.context:
Two weeks of HR attrition analysis is now ready to be packaged into deliverables. This week follows the same pattern as weeks 8 and 9 of the Superstore project, but the audience is different and the difference matters.

The Superstore analysis went to a retail executive who cares about revenue and margin. The HR attrition analysis goes to an HR Director who cares about retention, wellbeing, and culture -- and who is sensitive to how findings are framed. An analysis that says "the Sales department has a 35% attrition rate" lands differently than "35% of the Sales team left last year, costing approximately $2.1M in replacement costs." The second framing connects the attrition data to a business number the HR Director can bring to the CFO.

The dashboard for HR analysis has a different design pattern from a retail dashboard. The headline KPI is not revenue or margin -- it is the overall attrition rate, the number of at-risk employees, and the estimated annual cost. The filter-driven design is more important here because HR Directors typically need to slice by Department, Role, and Manager separately. A slicer that lets them click on "Sales" and see all the charts update is more useful than six charts for six departments.

The recommendations this week must be specific and paired with difficulty-and-impact ratings. "Increase salaries" is a recommendation but not a useful one because it conflicts with "reduce costs" that the CFO will bring to the same meeting. "Conduct mandatory 18-month tenure reviews for employees in the Sales role earning under $3K per month" is specific enough to schedule, budget, and evaluate.

By Sunday: a one-page filter-driven Excel dashboard, the HR Director memo (two pages, with the cost framing), and the five-slide deck with recommendations rated by difficulty and impact.

days.title: What HR actually needs
days.summary: Same packaging discipline, different audience. HR acts on people, privacy, and fairness.

items.title: What HR actually needs
items.body:
## What it is
You're packaging two weeks of attrition analysis into deliverables — like Superstore W8-9, but the audience is **HR leadership**, and that changes everything you emphasise.

## Why it matters
A sales director wants dollars; HR wants **actions on people**, framed around **retention, privacy, and fairness**. They don't care about your p-value; they care "which team do we help, and is this analysis fair to individuals?" Lead with the at-risk group and the intervention, not the methodology. Get the framing wrong and a technically perfect analysis gets ignored — or worse, raises legal/ethical flags (you must never single out *named* employees as flight risks).

## The rule for this audience
Talk about *groups and drivers* (overtime, early-tenure Sales Reps), never individuals. Recommend *policy* (cap overtime, fix onboarding), and acknowledge fairness (is the model just flagging a protected group?).

items.title: Build the dashboard
items.body:
## What it is
A **dashboard** is a single screen that answers the recurring questions at a glance — here, 4 KPI numbers (overall attrition, highest-risk department, overtime effect, first-year rate) plus 3 charts (by department, by tenure, by role).

## Why it matters
HR will check this monthly; they need the state of attrition in five seconds, not a notebook to run. A dashboard turns your one-off analysis into a *living instrument*. The discipline is restraint: a dashboard with 20 charts is as useless as none — pick the few numbers that drive decisions and make them unmissable.

## The layout
Top row: 4 big KPI numbers. Below: 3 charts (the department bar, the tenure survival curve, the role hotspot). One screen, no scrolling. Build it in Excel/Sheets or a notebook — the principle is the same.

items.title: Make it interactive (filters)
items.body:
## What it is
Add a **filter** (a slicer in Excel/Sheets, or a dropdown) so the viewer can slice the dashboard — e.g. show attrition for one department or one job level — without asking you.

## Why it matters
Static dashboards generate a flood of "can you also show me just Sales?" requests. A filter hands that power to HR, which makes the dashboard *self-serve* — the difference between a report you maintain forever and a tool they own. Self-serve dashboards are what get adopted; static ones get a glance and forgotten.

## The pattern
One or two filters max (department, job level). More than that and it's a control panel nobody understands. Wire the charts to respond to the filter so the whole screen updates together.

The memo is what circulates to people who never open the dashboard. weeks.context:
Three weeks of HR attrition analysis ends this week the same way the Superstore project ended: with a deliberate close, a retrospective, and a demo video that proves the project works.

The demo video is two to three minutes. Open the dashboard, click the Department slicer to show Sales, call out the attrition rate and the cost number, click to R&D and note the contrast. The SQL version of the HR analysis is the second deliverable this week. Every pivot table and calculated metric from weeks 10 through 12 should be expressible as a SQL query. items.creator: Fireship

items.title: See it in code (with output)
items.body:
## Attrition rate by department, in SQL
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```sql
SELECT Department,
       AVG(CASE WHEN Attrition='Yes' THEN 1.0 ELSE 0 END) AS attrition_rate,
       COUNT(*) AS employees
FROM hr GROUP BY Department ORDER BY attrition_rate DESC;
```
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```
Department              attrition_rate  employees
Sales                   0.206           446
Human Resources         0.190            63
Research & Development  0.138           961
```
Matches your pandas Week 10 result exactly — `AVG(CASE WHEN ...)` is the SQL of the 0/1 `left` mean.

weeks.title: Web scraping for business data
weeks.context:
Both projects so far used clean, pre-packaged datasets. Most real-world analyst work does not. Prices change on competitor websites. Product listings appear and disappear. Public datasets are updated irregularly. The skill of pulling structured data from unstructured web pages -- web scraping -- is not a developer skill, it is an analyst skill, and it is used constantly by anyone doing competitive intelligence, market research, or pricing analysis.

The context this week is competitor price tracking. You will choose a public website that lists prices -- a retailer's product page, a job board's salary listings, a real estate listing site, or a public government data portal -- and write a BeautifulSoup scraper that extracts the relevant fields, appends a row to a CSV with a timestamp, and can be run again tomorrow to capture the new prices.

The ethics of scraping matter and they are not complicated. Do not scrape sites that explicitly forbid it in their robots.txt. Do not scrape at a rate that burdens the server (add a 1-second delay between requests). Do not scrape personal data. Public product prices, public job listings, and public government data are generally acceptable. If you are unsure, read robots.txt before writing any code.

BeautifulSoup is the tool. It parses HTML and lets you find elements by tag, class, or ID. The workflow: requests.get(url) to fetch the page, BeautifulSoup(html, 'html.parser') to parse it, soup.find_all('div', class_='price') to extract the relevant elements. The elements change when the site redesigns -- your scraper is fragile by design, and knowing that it is fragile is part of the skill.

By Sunday: a competitor-price-tracker repo with a working scraper, an append-only history.csv that has at least 2 rows (two runs on different days), and a simple Google Sheets dashboard visualising the price history.

items.title: Why analysts scrape
items.body:
## What it is
Both projects used clean, packaged datasets. Most real analyst work doesn't get that gift — the data you need (competitor prices, listings, public stats) lives on **web pages**, not in a tidy CSV. **Web scraping** is programmatically extracting that data into a table you can analyse.

## Why it matters
Scraping unlocks questions no packaged dataset can answer: "how did our competitor's prices move this month?" There's no CSV for that — but there's a web page, updated daily, that you can turn into one. The analyst who can build their own dataset isn't limited to questions someone already answered. It's the difference between consuming data and *sourcing* it.

## The shape of it
Three steps: fetch the page (HTML), parse it to pull the values you want, and write them to a DataFrame/CSV. This week: ethics first, then BeautifulSoup, then schedule it, then analyse the result.

items.title: Scrape ethically (robots.txt)
items.body:
## What it is
Before scraping, check the site's **robots.txt** (e.g. `example.com/robots.txt`) and Terms of Service. Respect what's disallowed, identify yourself, and don't hammer the server.

## Why it matters
Scraping carelessly can be rude (overloading a small site), against ToS, or in some cases legally risky. A professional scrapes *politely*: obeys robots.txt, rate-limits requests (a pause between them), scrapes only public data, and never republishes copyrighted content. This isn't just ethics — a scraper that gets your IP banned is also useless. Doing it right keeps the data flowing and keeps you out of trouble.

items.title: BeautifulSoup hello world
items.body:
## What it is
`requests` fetches a page's HTML; **BeautifulSoup** parses it so you can pull out the elements you want by their tag/class. Together they're the standard beginner scraping toolkit.

## Why it matters
This is the core skill: turning a wall of HTML into the three values you actually care about. Once you can `find`/`find_all` the right elements, scraping any simple page is the same pattern — inspect the page to find the tag, then extract it. Start on a scraping-practice site (like books.toscrape.com), never a site that forbids it.

items.title: See it in code (with output)
items.body:
## Fetch a page and extract data
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```python
import requests
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup

url = "https://books.toscrape.com/"        # a scraping-practice site
html = requests.get(url, headers={"User-Agent": "learn-scraper"}).text
soup = BeautifulSoup(html, "html.parser")

books = soup.find_all("article", class_="product_pod")
for b in books[:3]:
    title = b.h3.a["title"]
    price = b.find("p", class_="price_color").text
    print(title, "|", price)
```
Output:
```
A Light in the Attic | £51.77
Tipping the Velvet | £53.74
Soumission | £50.10
```
You just turned a web page into structured data. `find_all` got every book block; inside each, `find`/attribute access pulled the title and price.

items.title: Schedule the scraper

## What it is
Save your scraper as a `.py` script and run it automatically on a schedule (Windows Task Scheduler / cron) so it captures the data **over time** — appending each run's results with a date.

## Why it matters
A one-off scrape is a snapshot; a *scheduled* scrape is a **time series**, which is where the real insight lives ("prices rose 12% this month"). Automating it also means the dataset builds itself while you sleep — the analyst's leverage. The key habit: stamp each row with the scrape date and append, never overwrite.

weeks.title: Project 3 — Marketing Funnel v0.1
weeks.context:
Project 3 uses real e-commerce data. The Olist dataset is a public Brazilian e-commerce dataset containing 100,000 orders from 2016 to 2018, with tables for orders, order items, payments, reviews, customers, sellers, and products. It is multi-table, which is meaningfully different from the single-table datasets you have worked with so far -- the analysis requires JOINs before it can answer most questions.

The marketing funnel question is: at each stage of the purchase journey, how many potential customers make it to the next stage, and where are the biggest drops? In a traditional e-commerce context the funnel is: visitor → product view → add to cart → checkout → purchase. The Olist data does not have visitor and view data, but it has order status (pending, processing, shipped, delivered, cancelled) and review data, which gives you a funnel from order placed to delivery to satisfaction.

The delivery-to-review connection is the most interesting question in this dataset. Olist is a marketplace -- sellers ship directly to customers, and delivery experience is entirely in the hands of third-party logistics. Review scores are the customer satisfaction signal. The question is whether delivery time (purchase date to delivery date) predicts review score. If it does, then late deliveries are not just an operational problem -- they are a reputation problem, and the analysis can quantify how much each day of delay costs in terms of review score.

This week is the exploration phase. You are not building the final dashboard yet -- you are understanding the schema, building the order status funnel, and computing the delivery-to-review correlation as a first signal. By the end of the week you will know whether there is a real story here, and you will have the building blocks for the deeper analysis in week 16.

By Sunday: schema diagram (a visual or written description of all seven tables and their join keys), the order status funnel computed, the delivery time distribution computed, and the delivery-review correlation with a scatter plot committed to a new olist-funnel-analysis repo.

items.title: What is a funnel?
items.body:
## What it is
Project 3 uses **Olist** — a public Brazilian e-commerce dataset: ~100,000 orders (2016-2018) across multiple tables (orders, items, customers, reviews, payments). A **funnel** tracks how customers progress through stages (ordered -> shipped -> delivered -> reviewed), and where they drop off.

## Why it matters
Every drop-off is lost money, and the funnel shows *exactly where*. "We lose customers somewhere" is useless; "8% of orders never reach delivered" points at a fixable operations problem. Funnel thinking is the core of marketing and e-commerce analytics — and Olist's multi-table structure forces you to practise the `merge` skill on realistic, messy, relational data.

## What's new here
Unlike Superstore (one table), Olist is **relational** — answers require *joining* tables. That's this project's growth edge: real data is normalised across tables, and you'll live in `merge`.

This is the project's core skill: real questions ("do late deliveries get worse reviews?") need columns from *different* tables, so you must join them correctly. The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```
band
```

weeks.title: Olist Funnel v0.2: Cohorts + repeat purchase
weeks.context:
Last week you found that delivery time correlates with review score. This week you move to a different marketing question: do Olist customers come back, and if so, what predicts whether they will?

Cohort analysis is the analyst's tool for measuring retention. A cohort is a group of customers who made their first purchase in the same time period -- the January 2017 cohort, the Q2 2017 cohort. By tracking each cohort through time, you can see whether customers acquired in different periods retained at different rates, and whether the business is getting better or worse at keeping customers over time.

The repeat purchase rate for Olist is surprisingly low. In most marketplaces, 30-40% of customers make a second purchase within 12 months. Olist is a B2C marketplace where many purchases are one-time (furniture, specific electronics, gifts) rather than recurring (groceries, consumables). The repeat rate you compute will probably be below 10%, and that is not necessarily a failure -- it is the nature of the product category mix. Knowing this matters for the marketing memo, because strategies optimised for repeat purchase (loyalty programmes, subscription offers) are less relevant for a low-repeat-purchase marketplace than strategies optimised for acquisition and first-purchase satisfaction.

The behavioral comparison between one-time and repeat buyers is where the interesting signal lives. Do repeat buyers rate deliveries higher? Do they come from different product categories? Do they have faster delivery times? These questions connect the delivery-review analysis from week 15 to the retention question.

By Sunday: a cohort retention matrix showing month-1 and month-3 retention by acquisition cohort, the overall repeat purchase rate computed correctly, the behavioral comparison table, and a one-paragraph write-up of the key finding for the marketing funnel memo.

items.title: What's a cohort?
items.body:
## What it is
A **cohort** is a group of customers defined by a shared start — usually their **first-purchase month**. Cohort analysis tracks each group's behaviour over the months that follow, to see if and when customers come back.

## Why it matters
A single "repeat rate" hides whether retention is improving or decaying over time. Cohorts answer the sharper question: "of customers who first bought in January, how many bought again in month 2, month 3…?" — and whether newer cohorts retain better than older ones (is the business getting healthier?). It's the gold-standard retention tool in marketing and SaaS, and the reason VCs ask for "cohort curves".

## The shape
Rows = cohort (first-purchase month); columns = months since first purchase; cells = % of that cohort still active. A retention *matrix*.

items.title: The cohort retention matrix
items.body:
## What it is
Build the matrix: for each order compute **months since the cohort start**, then `pivot_table` count of active customers by cohort (rows) × months-since (columns), converted to a % of each cohort's month-0 size.

## Why it matters
This single table is the deliverable of the week — it shows the retention *curve* for every cohort at once. Reading across a row shows decay; reading down a column shows whether newer cohorts retain better than older ones. It's the most information-dense retention artefact you can produce, and pivoting is exactly the Week-2 skill scaled up.

## Deeper dive: The cohort retention matrix

There isn't a single short video that nails this exact concept, so work it the way professionals actually learn it — by running small variations yourself and reading the output.

## Two more worked examples
1. Take the smallest case of **The cohort retention matrix** and predict the result *before* you run it. Then run it and compare — the gap between your prediction and reality is the learning.
2. Change one variable (a column, a parameter, a condition) and predict again. Repeat until your predictions are reliably right.

## What to watch for
- Trace the data through each step (split, apply, combine) rather than memorising syntax.
- Read the shape and the index of every intermediate result; most bugs are shape bugs.
- When stuck, shrink the input to 3 rows you can verify by hand.

items.title: See it in code (with output)
items.body:
## Build the retention matrix
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```python
o["months_since"] = ((o["order_month"] - o["cohort"]).apply(lambda x: x.n))
counts = o.pivot_table(index="cohort", columns="months_since",
                       values="customer_unique_id", aggfunc="nunique")
retention = counts.divide(counts[0], axis=0).round(3)
print(retention.iloc[:3, :4])
```
Output (illustrative):
```
months_since      0      1      2      3
cohort
2017-01        1.000  0.041  0.029  0.018
2017-02        1.000  0.038  0.025  0.021
2017-03        1.000  0.052  0.031  0.024
```
Read it: month-0 is always 100%; retention drops to ~4-5% by month 1. Olist's repeat behaviour is *low* (most customers buy once) — itself a key finding. Comparing down column 1, newer cohorts retain slightly better.

cards.whenRight: Right — normalise each cohort by its own month-0 size.
cards.whenWrong: It is — cells are % of the cohort's starting size.
